Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Amir was fifty-six years old, married, and worked as a social media manager for a mid-sized nonprofit. Eighteen months ago, on a cool October evening, he was driving home from the grocery store. A police cruiser’s lights flashed behind him as he pulled over for a broken taillight. The officer approached, asked for his license and registration, and then, without warning, ordered him out of the car. Before Amir could fully understand what was happening, he was on the ground, face pressed against cold asphalt, a knee grinding into his back. He remembers the sharp grit of gravel against his cheek, the metallic taste of blood from where his lip split against the pavement. He remembers pleading, “Please, I have a family,” and the officer’s indifferent silence. What stayed with him longest was not the pain but the shame of what he had said—the begging, the submission. It went against everything he believed about himself, about how a man should stand his ground.

In the months that followed, the memory would return without warning. Sometimes it arrived as a vivid taste of blood that filled his mouth, even when he was sitting safely in his living room. At other times, he felt a surge of rage so intense his hands would shake, the image of the officer’s boots filling his mind. But Amir learned to push the memory away before it could finish playing out—a sudden mental block, like slamming a door mid-scene. He did not want to see the rest.

His job became a minefield. As a social media manager, he curated content daily—news articles, videos, community posts. Any story about police brutality sent a jolt through him, and he began to avoid them entirely, scrolling past links, deleting reports from the queue, and eventually withdrawing from certain conversations at work. He stopped watching television dramas or films that involved conflict, and he no longer read the news. He told himself it was better not to feel anything—not the fear, not the guilt, not the rage—so he avoided anything that might stir an emotion, even positive ones like joy or pride, because those felt too close to vulnerability.

At home, his wife noticed the change. He became hypervigilant. When they went out to dinner, Amir would scan the room for exits, noting every door and window before he could sit down. Even in their own quiet house, he found himself checking the locks twice, three times, peering out the window before settling onto the couch. He could not relax, not even when he knew logically that no threat existed. The world, he had come to believe, was fundamentally dangerous. And people—even the ones who smiled at him—were not what they seemed. He no longer trusted kindness, interpreting every gesture as potentially hiding something.

What finally brought him to therapy was a moment at work that he could not shake. His supervisor had assigned him to monitor comments on a post about community policing. Amir froze, felt the familiar taste of blood in his mouth, and excused himself to the bathroom, where he stood for ten minutes gripping the sink, planning his escape route from the building even though he had no reason to flee. That evening, his wife found him sitting in the dark with the lights off, unable to explain why he was there. She urged him to talk to someone. He agreed, partly because he was exhausted, partly because he was terrified that the rage—the one that flared every time he let himself remember—might one day explode. He did not know if he could handle the full memory, but he was tired of living in fragments.
